h: India on climate: uncomfortable truths drowned out by applause
dek: Achin Vanaik says the praise for India at COP31 hid the fact that it is the world's third-largest emitter and stands among those blocking the road away from fossil fuels.
body: COP31 ended without a shared draft, yet India's role was widely praised at home. Achin Vanaik, a retired professor of international relations, believes India was right to raise the shortage of money for climate adaptation, but there was near silence on the fact that it opposed adding a gradual phase-out of fossil fuel production to the draft. This article first appeared in The India Cable.

According to the writer, India today is the third-largest annual emitter of greenhouse gases, after China and the US. He does not think it right to hide behind its 92nd rank in per capita emissions, because it is total emissions that heat the planet. On this basis he says India and China should give a far bigger share to the Loss and Damage Fund.

Another truth hides behind the per capita average. Vanaik estimates that the country's upper and middle class numbers 22 to 23 crore (220 to 230 million) even by the strictest measure, and 35 crore or more than 40 crore by looser measures. The consumption of this section vanishes into an average that includes the bottom half of the population.

Drawing on a study by Chancel and Piketty, he points out that the real income of the bottom half grew faster between 1951 and 1980 than in the period from 1981 to 2015, even though GDP growth was higher in the later period. According to the writer, after 2015, rising inequality and speeding environmental destruction, with forests cut, groundwater falling and glaciers melting, have gone hand in hand.

Vanaik sees the growing talk of carbon capture and geo-engineering as a distraction from the real work. In his view the least painful step is to stop new exploration and new production of fossil fuels. Denmark, Spain, Ireland and France have already banned new investment, while countries such as Norway, the US, Russia and China are going the other way, and India stands in that line too.
nazar: The language of climate justice that India speaks on world platforms is right: rich countries poured out smoke for centuries and now their money is not coming. But the same test should apply at home too. Heat, floods and sliding mountains hit Himalayan villages, coastal fishers, farm workers and city slums, while a large share of emissions belongs to the section whose consumption hides in the average.

Vanaik does not mean that India should give up coal overnight. He means there should be an accounting before the applause: development for whom, at whose cost, and with whose consent are new mines decided.
sawal: Whose smoke is hiding behind the per capita average?
ref: COP31
The 31st annual conference of the member countries of the UN climate treaty. This time it ended without any shared final draft.
Loss and Damage Fund
A fund to help vulnerable countries suffering destruction from the climate crisis. Agreement on it was reached at COP27 in Egypt in 2022.
ank: India's rank in annual greenhouse emissions
India's rank in per capita emissions

h: Plenty of profit, no risk: why Indian capital does not build the future
dek: Utkarsh Mishra writes that despite record profits and tax cuts, big business houses are putting money into easy-earning trades instead of factories and research.
body: The Finance Minister keeps telling industry to shed its hesitation and invest. The government cut corporate tax from 30 to 22 per cent, ran production-linked incentive schemes for 14 industries, and in the 2026-27 budget the Centre's capital spending reached a record 12.2 lakh crore rupees. Still, private corporate investment is stuck at 11 to 13 per cent of GDP, against about 17 per cent in 2007-08.

According to Ranchi journalist Utkarsh Mishra, the problem is not a lack of money. Profits of Nifty-500 companies were at a record 5.2 per cent of GDP in financial year 2026. The real point is that high earnings lie in businesses where competition is low or government approval is needed: ports, airports, spectrum, real estate, power and everyday goods. Instead of long-risk sectors such as semiconductors or AI, big houses are entering price wars over ten-rupee cold drinks and ice cream.

India spends less than one per cent of GDP on research, and close to half of that money still comes from the government. China, whose per capita income was similar to India's in the early 1990s, now spends 2.8 per cent, and industry provides a large part of it. Factory capacity use is stuck at 74 to 77 per cent because demand is weak: according to the writer, the real monthly earnings of salaried workers fell between 2012 and 2022.

Mishra suggests four reforms: tie tax breaks and subsidies to domestic research, technology and secure jobs; raise ordinary people's buying power through rural employment, a fair MSP (minimum support price) and public health and education; at least double the budget of universities and science institutions; and check the growing dominance of a few houses in the market.
nazar: This article is a reminder that the 'shortage of investment' is really a question of how power is shared. When profit comes from government approvals and control of markets, who needs to take risks? The price is paid by workers, whose wages are stuck, and by young people, for whom those factories and laboratories are simply not being built.
sawal: What future does a ten-rupee cold drink build?
ref: PLI scheme
The production-linked incentive scheme, under which companies get government money on increased output. It was brought into many industries after 2020.
Rent-seeking
Earning from government concessions, licences or control of a market without building anything new. Economics treats it as the opposite of productive investment.

h: The Narail fire: two homes burnt, three hundred on Indian channels
dek: Dhaka editor Faisal Mahmud explains how several Indian channels, without checking, presented a political clash in Bangladesh as an organised attack on Hindus.
body: On 18 November two BNP leaders were killed in Kalia upazila (sub-district) of Bangladesh's Narail district, and Awami League workers are accused. Two days later, homes of leaders and supporters linked to the Awami League were attacked. Faisal Mahmud, managing editor of Dhaka's Daily Wadah, reports that according to the local administration five or six homes were burnt and 15 to 20 were vandalised.

On many Indian channels and websites the picture was different. Some spoke of 300 Hindu homes burnt, some 200, some 100. The upazila officer confirmed that two homes were burnt: one belonging to a former Awami League MP, the other to a Hindu former upazila chairman linked to the party. Police say that no Hindu family even lives in Bendarchar village, where most of the violence took place, and that old and AI-made videos were spread. Office-bearers of the local puja committee and temple committee also rejected the claim that hundreds of Hindu homes were burnt.

According to the article, the Bangladeshi fact-checker The Dissent traced these claims to Facebook accounts linked to the Awami League and to at least ten Indian media outlets. Some English newspapers did print the police denial, but on many Bangla and Hindi platforms the unverified figures kept running.

Mahmud sees this as part of a pattern running since Sheikh Hasina's fall in August 2024. He also records that real attacks on minorities have happened, confirmed by BBC Verify, the United Nations and European agencies, in which political revenge and religious bias were tangled together. But according to an American research body, more than 90 per cent of over seven lakh (700,000) posts claiming a 'Hindu genocide' between August 2024 and January 2026 came from India.
nazar: The question of protecting minorities next door is real, and that is exactly why it must be kept safe from lies. Every exaggerated story weakens the voice of real victims and adds fuel to the fire of hatred inside India, for which Muslims here pay the price.
The lesson for newsrooms is simple: a figure from a party's social media account, without asking the police, the administration and local people, is not news.
sawal: If Bendarchar had no Hindu homes, whose homes burnt?
ref: Awami League
Sheikh Hasina's party, which lost power after the student movement of August 2024. Hasina has been in India since then.
BNP
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party, founded by Khaleda Zia and the old rival of the Awami League.

h: Six months of Vijay: popularity intact, a pile of questions for the government
dek: Senior journalist R. Rajagopalan writes that the TVK government's standing in Tamil Nadu still rests on Vijay's charisma, and January's six by-elections will be its first real test.
body: C. Joseph Vijay's TVK government in Tamil Nadu is in its sixth month. According to senior journalist and political analyst R. Rajagopalan, Vijay proved his majority in the Assembly, but his is a minority government that survives on the support of six parties: the Congress, VCK, CPI(M), CPI, IUML and MDMK. Allegations of MLAs being bought and sold are still in the air.

By-elections are due in the first fortnight of January 2027 for six seats: Perundurai, Ambasamudram, Viralimalai, Karur, Tiruchirappalli East and Kolathur. The writer sees them as a small referendum on the government. Kolathur is special, because there TVK MLA V.S. Babu had defeated M.K. Stalin, and after his death the way may open for Stalin to return to the Assembly.

Six months have brought six controversies. The Parandur airport project was cancelled. The decision to give free cars to all 234 MLAs backfired, because at the same time the government was citing tight funds and inherited debt for delays in welfare schemes. Allowances went up, and ruling MLAs were handed Diwali gifts at a Mahabalipuram resort. There were allegations that the industries department's investment information reached the Andhra Pradesh government, several prisoners escaped from jails and custody, and Vijay went to London to watch Ajith Kumar's car race at Silverstone.

According to Rajagopalan, the treasury is tight, the Supreme Court's Cauvery verdict went against the state, and Karnataka is moving ahead with the Mekedatu dam. Vijay has avoided a clash with the Centre. The writer concludes that charisma is still a shield, but solid proof of good governance is scarce, and law and order and his grip on his own MLAs are becoming major worries.
nazar: Popularity that comes from the cinema screen is nothing new in Tamil Nadu, but its test is always in governance. Cars and gifts for MLAs while welfare schemes are held up on the excuse of debt is the same old politics against which change was promised. The allied Left parties and the VCK have a duty to collect the price of their support in the form of work for ordinary people.
sawal: If welfare schemes stalled, from which treasury did the MLAs' cars come?
ref: TVK
Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam, the party actor Vijay formed in 2024. It formed the government in Tamil Nadu after the 2026 Assembly election.
Mekedatu
A proposed dam project on the Cauvery river in Karnataka. Tamil Nadu opposes it, fearing less water downstream.

h: Why is Russia asking for a map of all Europe in the Ukraine talks?
dek: Dimitar Bechev of Carnegie Europe asks what Moscow really wants by adding new conditions about Europe's security order to the Abu Dhabi talks.
body: The Trump administration wants to act as a go-between for Moscow and Kyiv to end a war that has gone on for almost five years. In early November, three-way talks restarted in Abu Dhabi, but not even an outline of a deal emerged. Instead, Russia put Europe's security arrangements on the table as a new dispute.

According to the writer, Russia wants NATO, in return for stopping attacks on Ukrainian cities, to pull its forces out of the countries on its eastern border and take in no new members. The demand is not new: in December 2021, a few weeks before the invasion, Moscow sent two draft treaties with similar conditions, which Washington rejected.

Now the list of conditions is longer: European military aid to Kyiv must stop, no foreign soldier may stay on Ukrainian soil, Finland must leave NATO and become neutral, and the nuclear umbrella of Britain and France must not extend to the rest of Europe. Bechev says this would mean reversing almost everything Europe has added to collective defence since February 2022. Even if Trump wanted to, he could not get Europe to accept this deal.

So why does Russia keep repeating it? A softer reading is that it has opened the bargaining at a high price, and that once the war stops, both sides will need some limits on military activity, contact between intelligence agencies and new life in a body like the OSCE. The second reading is more bitter: to spread the agenda, pull attention away from Ukraine and gain ground on the front line.

The writer recalls that Moscow puts relations among the great powers above regional issues, and the same thinking showed at the meeting of Putin, Trump and Xi in Shenzhen. Europeans are almost shut out of the talks. In his view the talk of a security order may well be a cover, yet avoiding war in Europe should be everyone's shared goal.
nazar: When great powers sit down to divide the world among themselves, those on whose land the war is being fought are the ones left outside the room. This complaint of Ukraine and Europe is nothing new for South Asia and Africa.

India buys oil and weapons from Russia and also manages its ties with the US. If meetings of the big three like the one in Shenzhen become a new habit, middle-sized countries, India among them, will have to think about where their voice will be heard.
sawal: If the war is in Ukraine, why is Finland's neutrality a condition?
ref: Abu Dhabi talks
Three-way talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine that restarted in the capital of the United Arab Emirates in November 2026, so far without producing any outline.
OSCE
The Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, which includes the EU countries, Russia and the US. It grew out of talks in the Cold War era.

h: The curtain falls on COP31: a failure that may become a new start
dek: Climate policy analyst Ayesha Khan writes that COP31 gave no solid result, but an open failure may be better than a weak agreement.
body: COP31 took place at a time when the world is struggling with geopolitical rifts, inflation and tight budgets, and the danger of crossing the 1.5 degree limit looms. The stakes were high, but according to the writer the talks did not move the agenda forward and the weaknesses of international cooperation came fully into view.

First, the lack of leadership. Host Türkiye and Australia, which chaired the talks, could not reach any major agreement. Even a watered-down draft failed to win consensus and was not passed. Big emitters made no firm promise to tighten their 2030 targets in line with the Paris Agreement.

The quarrel between rich and poor countries over responsibility and capacity stayed exactly where it was. Pledges for adaptation and for loss and damage were badly inadequate, climate finance neither grew nor got a clear route to reach people, and the framework for quick help after disasters did not move either. The demand for compensation got stuck in a political fight over liability. The biggest miss was that no clear roadmap for leaving fossil fuels was made, and behind this the writer sees entrenched economic interests.

Still, Ayesha Khan does not see this as the end of climate efforts, but as proof that the present method is not enough. She suggests adding accountability to the model in which countries make promises of their own choosing, and giving civil society, Indigenous communities and the private sector a place in the talks.

Her most interesting argument is that failed talks do less harm than a weak agreement that gives false comfort. She recalls the 2009 Copenhagen conference, whose disagreements led to the 2015 Paris Agreement. According to the writer, the failure of COP31 is really a victory for COP21.
nazar: Pakistan and India are both suffering floods, heatwaves and drought, and for both, money for adaptation is not a footnote of some conference but a question of life. At COP31 this was exactly the money that came in least.
The hope of seeing failure as a new start will come true only if poor countries press together with one voice. India too will have to move beyond defending its coal and become part of that pressure.
sawal: Paris came out of Copenhagen; what will come out of COP31?
ref: COP
The annual conference of the member countries of the UN climate treaty. The 2015 Paris Agreement was reached at COP21.
Loss and damage
The demand that rich, more polluting countries pay to make up for the losses poor countries suffer from climate disasters.

h: Pakistan's democracy did not collapse, it was brought down
dek: Starting from a remark by Bilawal Bhutto, Shazia Nizamani lays out a 79-year record in which no prime minister has completed five years.
body: On 17 November at the Karachi Press Club, PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said the system did not collapse, it was brought down. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi wants an administrative restructuring; Bilawal accepted the diagnosis but not the cure, and spoke of a reset that rests on the 2006 Charter of Democracy and begins in Parliament.

The writer tests this statement against history. To this day no prime minister in Pakistan has completed five years. In 1954 Governor-General Ghulam Muhammad dissolved the Constituent Assembly, and the court upheld it, giving birth to the doctrine of necessity. The One Unit scheme of 1955 erased the separate identities of Sindh, Balochistan and the Frontier without a mandate. In 1958 the court called Ayub Khan's coup a successful revolution.

In 1960 Ayub had himself confirmed through a yes-or-no referendum. In 1970, when Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Awami League won a majority, the Assembly was not allowed to meet, and within a year Bangladesh was born. In 1977 Zia-ul-Haq removed Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who was hanged in 1979; in March 2024 the Supreme Court accepted that he had not received a fair trial.

Using Article 58(2)(b), brought in by Zia's Eighth Amendment, four elected governments were removed between 1988 and 1999. The Eighteenth Amendment of 2010 removed that article and gave powers to the provinces, which is why Bilawal treats touching it as a red line. According to the writer, after that, governments were not dismissed but hollowed out through courts and disqualification: Gilani in 2012, Nawaz Sharif in 2017, and Imran Khan in 2022.

Shazia Nizamani says the debate should move from the failure of the system to who made it fail. The cure lies in the Constitution and Parliament, not in referendums, provinces made by decree, or governments removed from outside Parliament. She also notes that, even while in the coalition, Bilawal called Imran Khan a political prisoner.
nazar: This history next door reminds us that democracy often does not fall in one blow; courts, referendums and selective cases in the name of 'accountability' hollow it out slowly. The push to redraw the map is often a way to cover up that hollowness.

In India too, the debate over federalism, the division of states and cases against opposition leaders is alive. Pakistan's lesson is that every 'reset' done by pushing Parliament aside prepares the ground for the next dismissal.
sawal: Where no prime minister has lasted five years, who will do the reset?
ref: Doctrine of necessity

Nazariya-e-zaroorat: the argument, from the 1955 Tamizuddin Khan case, that under the pressure of circumstances even unconstitutional steps can be lawful. Military coups later drew legitimacy from it.
Charter of Democracy
A 2006 agreement between Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif, which promised to reject military interference, and to set up a constitutional court and an independent election commission.

h: Are journalists without accreditation less protected? Supreme Court to examine
dek: In the case of journalists removed from anti-CEC protests, the court asked who a journalist really is and how much protection they have.
body: Delhi Police allegedly detained and forcibly removed journalists covering protests that demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The Supreme Court heard petitions on this from the Kerala Union of Working Journalists, the Network of Women in Media, the Free Speech Collective and the Delhi Union of Journalists. A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana said it would examine whether accredited journalists get more legal protection than those who call themselves journalists. During the hearing Justice Bagchi remarked that people who describe themselves as journalists may not get the same protection.

The bench kept three questions open: who should count as a journalist, and whether accreditation or links with an organisation should decide their protection; whether a journalist has any special leeway before the police while covering a protest; and whether forcibly removing a journalist from a protest site amounts to detention. The court said press freedom has to be weighed against public order.

The KUWJ petition was disposed of, and the allegations of mistreatment and detention of seven journalists were sent to an inquiry committee set up by the court. They include reporters from 24News, Asianet, Reporter TV, Mathrubhumi and Manorama News, and an independent journalist, Farasana. Delhi Police had said in an affidavit that influencers and reel makers would not get the same protection as accredited journalists. The petitioners cite the order of 11 October, which said the work of lawyers and journalists must not be obstructed.
nazar: Journalism is known by the work, not by a government card. Today ground reports often come from independent and small journalists who have neither accreditation nor a big organisation. If the line of protection is drawn at accreditation, the police will get the power to decide who may watch and who may not.
sawal: Will a journalist dragged away from a protest count as detained?
ref: Accredited journalist
A journalist who has an identity card from the government's Press Information Bureau or a state information department. Most journalists from independent and small outlets do not have one.

h: Father's name struck off, newborn daughter's birth certificate held up
dek: In Cooch Behar, a two-and-a-half-month-old girl cannot get a birth certificate because her father's name was removed in the SIR and he was called a Bangladeshi.
body: Amina Khatun of Khatamari village in West Bengal's Cooch Behar district gave birth to a daughter on 9 September at Dinhata Sub-Divisional Hospital. Citing a report in The Hindu, Maktoob says that when she and her husband Abdul Habib went to the hospital and the panchayat office for a birth certificate, they were told first to bring verification of residence from the pradhan (village head) or the MLA.

The office of Dinhata MLA Ajay Roy refused, on the ground that Habib's name had been struck off the voter list in the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR. Habib says he was called a Bangladeshi there and told first to register in the NRC, although he has lived here since birth and his grandfather built the family home in the village. The Sahebganj BDO (block development officer) also returned the application for the same reason.

The names of Habib's three sisters have also been struck off. The commission had summoned them over a 'logical discrepancy', saying six other people had listed their father as their own father. The names of Habib's parents, wife and elder sister remain on the list. Habib has appealed to a tribunal to restore his name, and the appeal is still pending.

The Association for Protection of Civil Rights has said that registering a birth is a legal duty and a child's identity cannot be tied to the electoral status of the parents. The organisation will file a legal application with the District Magistrate. The SIR in Bengal had removed 91 lakh (9.1 million) names.
nazar: Losing a name from the voter list is no longer just the loss of a vote; it is spreading to rations, schemes and now to the proof of a baby girl's birth. Declaring someone a foreigner on the basis of a process whose appeal is not even complete is not the administration's job. The newborn should get her certificate at once, without conditions.
sawal: Who will ask a two-and-a-half-month-old baby for proof of citizenship?
ref: Logical discrepancy
The commission's term in the SIR for when someone's details do not seem to match, such as one person recorded as the father of many people. Such voters were sent notices for a hearing.
Birth registration
Under the law on registration of births and deaths, every birth must be recorded. Article 7 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child also gives the right to immediate registration.

h: No data on voters by religion, says UP's election officer
dek: On Yogi Adityanath's claim that 1.25 crore Hindu voters went missing, the Chief Electoral Officer said the commission does not even record religion or caste.
body: Uttar Pradesh's Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa told the Indian Express that the Election Commission has no data on voters by religion and has shared no such data with Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath. Adityanath had claimed that 1.2 crore (12 million) Hindu voters were left out of the list in the SIR and that Muslim voters rose by 1.6 per cent. The source of his figures is not clear.

On 13 November, SP chief Akhilesh Yadav had asked the commission where the Chief Minister got this figure of deleted voters, calling it a conspiracy to spread fear in society. According to Rinwa, about 2.5 crore eligible people in the state are off the list, but their religion or caste cannot be found out, because the database can only be sorted by things like gender and age, and Form 6 has no box for religion or caste.

Asked whether the commission had asked the Chief Minister for the basis of his claim, Rinwa called the question a misreading of the situation. He said he has no data either to confirm the claim or to deny it, and he does not think the Chief Minister is questioning the commission.

A Special Summary Revision is now under way in the state. Claims and objections can be filed until 16 December, and the final list will be published on 4 January. By 17 November, more than 18.8 lakh (1.88 million) people had been added to the draft list.
nazar: When the commission itself says it has no data on religion, a Chief Minister presenting a count by religion is like turning the voter list into a communal campaign. Instead of quietly sidestepping this, the commission should say plainly that such a claim rests on none of its records.
sawal: If the form has no box for it, how did the figure reach the Chief Minister?
ref: Chief Electoral Officer
The Election Commission's top officer in each state, who oversees the voter list and the running of elections.

h: Wrong to shut an NGO in the name of secret intelligence: Delhi High Court
dek: The court struck down the Home Ministry's 2022 order cancelling the FCRA registration of the Socio-Legal Information Centre.
body: Justice Anup Jairam Bhambhani of the Delhi High Court rebuked the Home Ministry because the security inputs on which the foreign contribution registration of the Socio-Legal Information Centre, or SLIC, was cancelled were not shown even to the court. The government said it learnt of the violations through secret security inputs that could not be disclosed. The court said such inputs cannot be kept so secret that nothing at all comes before the court, especially when they led to the registration being ended.

The ministry cancelled the registration on 17 October 2022 after an audit; as early as February 2022 it had been suspended and the accounts frozen. The allegations were that the organisation paid the bar association fees of lawyers Colin Gonsalves and Gayatri Singh, paid office rent to Gonsalves, and used foreign contributions on training in South Asian countries. The government had also said the organisation creates a false image of India's institutions in the eyes of the international community, which the court called baseless and beyond belief.

The court called the order illegal and far harsher than needed. Under Section 14(2) of the FCRA, a personal hearing is required before cancellation; a show-cause notice alone is not enough. The judge said an organisation that had worked for people on the margins for three decades, with no earlier complaint against it, was almost finished off by this decision. SLIC can apply for renewal, and the government must decide soon without relying on those allegations.
nazar: In recent years the FCRA has been used again and again against organisations that question the government. No hearing and no evidence in the name of a secret file is not a way of governing, it is a way of punishing. Relief has come four years after the decision, but no one will answer for the people whose legal aid stopped during these years.
sawal: Why should an organisation die on evidence even judges cannot see?
ref: FCRA
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act. Every organisation that takes donations from abroad must get registration from the Home Ministry, and once it is cancelled the organisation's money stops.
Socio-Legal Information Centre
An organisation that describes itself as providing legal aid and education, and has fought cases for people on the margins for three decades.

h: Allahabad High Court's hijab ruling will not be a precedent: Supreme Court
dek: The Supreme Court barred the ruling, given in the case of a student denied admission at a Prayagraj school, from being treated as a precedent.
body: The Supreme Court has said that the Allahabad High Court's ruling of 21 August, which said covering the head is not an essential religious practice of Islam, will not be treated as a precedent in other cases. Scroll reported this citing LiveLaw.

The case began with the petition of a student who wanted to wear a hijab with her school uniform. She alleged that Tagore Public School in Prayagraj refused her admission to Class 11 because of her headscarf. The High Court had said nothing on record suggested that a Muslim girl who does not wear a hijab would be considered outside the religion.

The Muslim Women's Study Circle argued in the Supreme Court that the ruling goes against constitutional rights such as equality, expression, freedom of religion and protection from discrimination, is arbitrary, and blocks Muslim girls' path to education. The petition also said that it is treated differently from other religious symbols such as the Sikh turban, and that the Quran directs the hijab.

On 20 November the court had issued notice on another petition by an organisation of Muslim women and tagged it with the pending appeals against the Karnataka High Court ruling that upheld the state government's ban on the hijab in educational institutions. A larger bench has yet to decide these appeals.
nazar: From Karnataka to Prayagraj, the debate stays tangled in theology, while the real question is whether a girl got to sit in class or not. The Supreme Court has for now stopped this ruling from spreading, but until the larger bench speaks, for many girls the school door will open only on the condition of the scarf.
sawal: Which school is that Class 11 student studying in now?
ref: Essential religious practice

A test made by the courts: whether a custom is so necessary a part of a religion that without it the religion's nature would change. This decides whether it gets protection under Article 25 of the Constitution.
Karnataka hijab case
In 2022 the Karnataka High Court upheld a ban on the hijab in schools and colleges. A two-judge bench of the Supreme Court gave a split verdict and the case is with a larger bench.

h: Trade in poor women's eggs in Hyderabad puts clinics under scrutiny
dek: Raids found about 40 women, mostly Muslim and Dalit women from other states, brought with the lure of money to have their eggs taken again and again.
body: Mariam (name changed) from West Bengal and her husband, a madrasa teacher, had a debt of one lakh rupees. Through a friend, an agent, Nikhat Parveen, promised 50,000 to 70,000 rupees for each egg retrieval. On 10 October she reached Hyderabad at her own cost and hormone injections began, but before the procedure her hostel in Begumpet was raided. After two weeks in a shelter home she went back to Kolkata empty-handed, with her papers seized for the investigation.

In raids on hostels in Begumpet and Saroornagar on 30 October, about 40 women from several states were found, mostly Muslim or Dalit, from poor families. According to the police, agents gathered women through sub-agents in other states, and some women had their eggs taken repeatedly by moving them around several clinics so that no record was made. The FIR names five clinics, including Oasis, Fertilica and Nova, with charges of trafficking, cheating and breaking the ART law.

Health officials found agreements between an ART bank linked to Oasis and nine middlemen, with terms of paying up to 65,000 rupees per donor and halving the amount if fewer than seven eggs were retrieved. The bank recorded 66 egg retrievals from January to October, but showed papers for only 47. According to Women's Commission chairperson Nerella Sharada, more than 90 per cent of the donors at most clinics were from outside. On 24 November the High Court rejected the doctors' anticipatory bail pleas, and on 25 November the commission asked the Governor for a special investigation.
nazar: The law bans selling eggs and bans middlemen, yet the bodies of women drowning in debt became a market in which brokers, hostels and clinics all seem linked. If arrests stop at the agents, this trade will rise again. For the women who were rescued, returning their papers, giving them treatment and paying compensation is also the government's duty.
sawal: Where are the 19 women whose papers were not found?
ref: ART (Regulation) Act, 2021
The law that governs assisted reproductive technology such as IVF. It bans selling eggs or sperm and bans middlemen, and a woman may donate only once in her life, at most seven eggs.
ART bank
An organisation that screens donors and stores eggs and sperm. Both clinics and banks must register with the National ART and Surrogacy Registry.

h: At Nagpur people's court, families of campus casteism victims testify
dek: At the first people's court on caste discrimination in higher education, the families of Sahil Wakode, Payal Tadvi, Anita and Raghavi told their stories.
place: Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar International Convention Centre, Nagpur
ask: Pass a Rohith Act and declare institutional casteism a crime
body: On 22 November, a one-day people's court (jan adalat) on caste discrimination in higher education was held in Nagpur, which the organisers called the first hearing of its kind in the country. It was organised by the All India Independent Scheduled Castes Association, led by its president Dr. Rahul Sonpimple. The jury was chaired by Prof. Sukhadeo Thorat, former chairman of the UGC.

The parents of Sahil Wakode, who lost his life at IIT Bombay in September, said their son had accused a professor of threatening him over his caste. A case has been filed against the professor under the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act, but there has been no arrest. The IIT denies the allegations of discrimination. Payal Tadvi's mother said that even after seven years the trial has not begun, and Raghavi's father said there has not been a single hearing in the High Court in four years.

Six Dalit and backward-class students expelled from the Hindi university in Wardha also testified. According to figures placed in the Lok Sabha, of 45 suicides at IITs between 2020 and 2025, 28 were of SC, ST and OBC students. The jury issued a 15-point resolution, demanding an independent complaints body on every campus with half its members from SC/ST communities, and an annual social audit.
nazar: When the police, the courts and the university are all silent, families testifying before the public is democracy's last window. If equal opportunity cells survive only to celebrate birth anniversaries, then even ten years after Rohith Vemula the lesson has not been learnt.
sawal: Why were 28 of the 45 suicides at IITs students from deprived communities?
ref: Rohith Vemula
A Dalit research scholar at the University of Hyderabad whose suicide in 2016 led to demands for a law against caste discrimination on campuses.
Equal opportunity cell
A unit every university must set up under the UGC's 2012 rules, meant to hear complaints of discrimination.

h: Six years on, farmers from Patiala to Delhi demand an MSP law
dek: The Samyukt Kisan Morcha held protests across the country on Thursday; in Delhi, police did not allow the march.
ask: A legal guarantee of MSP at C2+50% and assured procurement
body: Organisations linked to the Samyukt Kisan Morcha (United Farmers' Front) held protests at more than a hundred places across the country on Thursday, 26 November, the sixth anniversary of the farmers' movement that began on Delhi's borders. The organisations say most of the written assurances the Centre gave on 9 December 2021 have still not been kept.

In Punjab, rallies were held in Patiala, Bathinda, Jalandhar and Amritsar. According to the Morcha's statement, farmers from seven districts of Malwa gathered at PUDA Ground in Patiala, and 15 organisations took part. In Delhi, farmers set out from Mandir Marg towards Jantar Mantar, but police said permission had not been given and imposed prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the BNSS.

Vijoo Krishnan, general secretary of the All India Kisan Sabha, said the main demand is a law for MSP at C2+50% and assured procurement. Other demands include withdrawing the proposed India-US trade deal, loan waivers, Rs 25 lakh for the families of farmers and farm workers who died by suicide, withdrawal of all four labour codes, 200 days of rural work a year at a daily wage of Rs 700, and a sugarcane price of Rs 500 a quintal. The Morcha condemned the attack on Amal Haldar, vice-president of the Kisan Sabha, in Bardhaman, and blamed BJP supporters for it.
nazar: If the same charter of demands has to be repeated after six years, it raises a question about what a written promise is worth. That a movement which forced the government to withdraw laws was not even allowed to mark its anniversary in the capital shows that the government has learnt to trust barricades more than talks.
sawal: How many of the written assurances of 9 December 2021 have been kept?
ref: The Swaminathan Commission formula: the full cost of farming, plus land rent and interest on capital, with a 50 per cent profit on top.

h: Anganwadi workers sit in at Bhubaneswar, 74,000 centres shut
dek: The workers, who want government employee status and better pay, had their issue raised in the Assembly by both the ruling side and the opposition.
ask: Government employee status, Rs 30,000 for workers and Rs 15,000 for helpers
body: About 74,000 anganwadi centres in Odisha stayed shut on Thursday for the fourth day in a row. Led by the All Odisha Anganwadi Ladies Workers' Association, workers and helpers are on a sit-in on Mahatma Gandhi Marg near the Assembly with a seven-point charter of demands.

They want workers and helpers to be treated as government employees, a monthly honorarium of Rs 30,000 for workers and Rs 15,000 for helpers, and gratuity and retirement benefits. After a raise in 2023, a worker now gets Rs 10,000, a mini anganwadi worker Rs 7,250 and a helper Rs 5,000.

During Zero Hour on Thursday, BJD MLA Dhruba Charan Sahu said the centres had come to a standstill and that Deputy Chief Minister and Women and Child Development Minister Pravati Parida was abroad. He reminded the House that the BJP had promised Rs 25,000 before the 2024 election, and demanded that the workers be recognised as workers so they get at least the minimum wage of Rs 18,000. BJP MLA Bhaskar Madhei also spoke for raising the honorarium and reopening the centres at once. The report carries no official statement from the government. On Thursday the women on the sit-in also performed the Manabasa Gurubar puja right there.
nazar: Women who carry the nutrition of children and the care of mothers on their shoulders are called volunteers and paid half a wage. That is the official way of exploitation. That 74,000 centres had to close to remind the government of an election promise says a lot about its priorities.
sawal: What will the government say now about its election promise of Rs 25,000?
ref: Anganwadi
Village and neighbourhood centres under the Integrated Child Development Services scheme, where young children, pregnant women and mothers get nutrition, vaccination and early learning.

h: Hundreds of Paharia Adivasis sit in at the Pakur collectorate
dek: The Adim Janjati Vikas Samiti sent ten demands to the President, including recognition of the Malto language and two per cent reservation.
ask: Recognition for the Malto and Mabdo languages, 2% reservation for primitive tribes
body: On 25 November, hundreds of people from the Paharia community held a one-day sit-in at the collectorate premises in Jharkhand's Pakur district. The sit-in was held under the banner of the Akhil Bharatiya Adim Janjati Vikas Samiti (All India Primitive Tribes Development Committee). According to the report, 500 to 700 people came from remote villages of the district. It was led by Shivcharan Malto, secretary of the committee and a former zila parishad member.

Addressing the gathering, Malto alleged that the state government is doing injustice to primitive tribes, that their rights are being steadily cut and that their problems are not taken seriously. The committee's demands include adding the Malto and Mabdo languages to the state's list of tribal languages, two per cent reservation for primitive tribes, a monthly pension of Rs 2,500 for women, and a representative of the community on the Jharkhand Tribes Advisory Council.

At the end of the sit-in, the committee handed the Deputy Commissioner a ten-point memorandum addressed to the President. Malto warned that if there is no positive reply soon, there will be a sit-in before the Commissioner in Dumka on 30 December, followed by an indefinite hunger strike before the Governor in Ranchi. The report records no response from the government or the administration.
nazar: The Paharia are among the communities that government files count as the most vulnerable, yet they have to walk to the district headquarters to get their own language recognised. That the primitive tribes themselves have no voice on the Tribes Advisory Council is a big question in itself.
sawal: Why is there still no Paharia representative on the Tribes Advisory Council?
ref: Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups
The 75 communities, also called primitive tribes, that the Centre considers the most backward; in Jharkhand they include the Mal Paharia and Sauria Paharia.

h: Technical graduates in Kohima warn of a recruitment agitation from 30 November
dek: The Combined Technical Association of Nagaland had given the government until 26 November on the rules of the Staff Selection Board.
ask: All government recruitment through the NSSB, under transparent rules
body: The Combined Technical Association of Nagaland (CTAN), a body of young people with technical degrees, said at a press conference in Kohima that if the government does not accept its demands by 26 November, a peaceful, non-violent agitation will begin on 30 November. The organisation had given its first ultimatum on 21 September and its final ultimatum on 16 November.

CTAN has three demands. First, bring back the old rule of the Nagaland Staff Selection Board (NSSB) that fixed a minimum and maximum limit for interview marks, because, according to the organisation, removing it opens the way to arbitrary assessment. Second, departments and posts that are now outside the board's reach should be brought into the same process. The organisation cited alleged irregularities in recruitment in the excise and forest departments. Third, provisions of an office memorandum that, according to the organisation, weaken the powers of the NSSB and the school education board should be removed.

The organisation expressed anger at the delay in notifying a cabinet decision and questioned the slow pace of filling vacant posts on the board. It has appealed to unemployed youth, candidates and parents to join it.
nazar: In a state where a government job is the biggest source of employment, transparency in recruitment is a question for every household. By giving two ultimatums in three months, the young people have kept the door to talks open; replying is now the government's responsibility.
sawal: Why were excise and forest department recruitments kept outside the board?
ref: Nagaland Staff Selection Board
The body that holds exams and recruitment for the state government's non-gazetted jobs.

h: ASHA workers' sit-in at Bengaluru's Freedom Park enters its tenth day
dek: Thousands of ASHA workers paid an honorarium of Rs 5,000 are holding out for Rs 15,000 and a fixed salary.
ask: Honorarium raised from Rs 5,000 to Rs 15,000, a fixed salary and job security
body: Thousands of ASHA workers from Karnataka have been on an indefinite sit-in at Bengaluru's Freedom Park since 17 November, and their protest is reaching its tenth day. The sit-in is led by the Samyukta Karnataka ASHA Karyakarteyara Sangha. At present these workers get an honorarium of Rs 5,000 a month.

They want the honorarium raised to Rs 15,000 with a fixed salary, job and social security, payment of pending incentives, clearing of dues owed to retired workers, and a retirement benefit of Rs 5 lakh. They are also asking for financial help in illness and accidents, three months of paid leave for serious illness, Rs 5,000 for those who complete NIOS training, and reinstatement of workers who have left. The workers say they are forced to work through the 'Samastha' app, and want this stopped.

Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, who is on an official visit to Japan, appealed to them over a video call to end the sit-in, but the workers refused. They want the Chief Minister to come to Freedom Park himself and give a firm assurance. They also sang songs about the Chief Minister's absence. Police kept Seshadri Road closed all night to stop a march towards Vidhana Soudha. According to the report, no solution is in sight for now.
nazar: ASHA workers, who keep count of vaccines, births and illnesses in every village, are the backbone of the government's health system, yet they are treated as volunteers, not workers. Their work is being monitored through an app, but their pay is stuck at the same old scale.
sawal: If an app can monitor them, why not a salary of Rs 15,000?
ref: ASHA
Village and settlement-level health workers under the National Health Mission, who get an honorarium and task-based incentives instead of a salary.

h: The women of Ramni: rare mountain herbs now grown in fields
dek: In a high village of Uttarakhand, women farmers are growing dwindling herbs like kutki and atis, easing the pressure on the forest and running their homes.
body: In Uttarakhand's Ramni village, women are growing crops that usually grow wild, not in fields, on bugyals (high meadows) and slopes above two thousand metres. According to this Mongabay report, herbs like kutki, sugandhbala and atis are declining in the wild because of reckless wild harvesting, the growing demand of the drug industry and the difficulty of reaching high pastures. Scientists believe that growing them in fields can ease the pressure on wild populations.

The burden of this work falls mostly on women, because the village men leave to find work. According to scientists, these same women watch the crop most closely and are the first to report plant diseases.

The organisation Udyogini gets saplings from government institutions such as HRDI and the G.B. Pant Institute and distributes them. Each 200 square metre field gets two thousand saplings free. Some species have been replanted on degraded bugyals, and wild animals do not destroy them the way they do ordinary crops. Recently, 23 farmers sent one and a half lakh kutki cuttings to another village, yet by the scientists' reckoning cultivation meets only ten per cent of demand.

The road is not easy. Certification often needs land ownership, and very little land is in women's names, so Udyogini gets the certificates registered in the women's names. Kishan Singh Bhotia and Asha Devi Bhotia, who live near the India-China border, spend about two thousand rupees a trip to carry their produce to the road six kilometres away. These crops have no farm insurance, and the project money can stop at any time.
Even so, this income is paying for children's schooling and daily expenses, and the women farmers are proud that they are helping save the biodiversity of the Himalaya.
nazar: In the story of migration from the hills, the women who are left behind are the ones handling farming, conservation and the market, all three. But the land is not in their name, there is no insurance, no road, and the project money is temporary. If the government truly wants to promote herb farming, it must make women's land rights, crop insurance and help with transport part of policy; otherwise this labour will shrink into cheap raw material for drug companies.
sawal: How far would kutki farming spread if the land were in women's names?
ref: Bugyal
High mountain grasslands of Uttarakhand that serve as summer pastures. Many rare herbs grow wild here.
Kutki
A medicinal Himalayan herb (Picrorhiza kurroa) whose root is widely used in Ayurvedic medicines. Over-harvesting has made it scarce in the wild.

h: Cox's Bazar: lives on hold, in the month of Ramzan
dek: This Al Jazeera World film follows six Rohingya people in the world's largest refugee settlement, and Rohingya camera crew who live in the camp helped make it.
by: Al Jazeera World (with a Rohingya producer and cinematographer)
body: More than a million Rohingya refugees live in the camps of Cox's Bazar, at the southern tip of Bangladesh. This documentary of about 47 minutes, part of Al Jazeera's 'Al Jazeera World' series, was made from inside this settlement. According to the film's introduction, the team that made it included a Rohingya producer and a Rohingya cinematographer who live in the settlement themselves. So it is less the view of a journalist from outside and more the view of someone from within.

The film follows six people. A widowed mother who has recently fled Myanmar. A father who runs his home with a small trade in betel leaves. A student who also speaks up for the rights of his people. A painter, a musician, and a young man who has to hide his identity for his own safety.

The introduction calls their condition lives on hold. Food aid is shrinking, chances to work and study are very few, loved ones are separated and there is no clear way home. Through all this the month of Ramzan goes on, and the film shows fasting, prayer, family and the customs the settlement keeps together, alongside the growing hardship.

The background is well known. After the military crackdown in Myanmar's Rakhine state in August 2017, more than seven lakh (700,000) Rohingya crossed the border into Bangladesh, and together with the refugees already there, this became the world's largest refugee settlement. Since its 1982 citizenship law, Myanmar has not recognised the Rohingya as citizens, so most Rohingya are stateless.

In recent years, cuts in international aid have reduced rations in the camps, and Bangladesh has said again and again that it cannot carry the burden of so many people alone. The civil war in Myanmar and the fighting in Rakhine have pushed the idea of return even further away.

The film's emphasis is that even in such hardship people are working, studying, creating and holding their families together, so that their dignity survives. It is an attempt to show the faces behind the numbers.
nazar: In India the Rohingya are often spoken of in the language of infiltration and threat, while a few hundred kilometres away a million people live without a country, without work and on shrinking rations. What makes this film special is that the camera is in the hands of the people whose story it is.
Leaving Bangladesh alone to carry one of South Asia's biggest human tragedies is a failure of the whole region, and India is not free of it.
sawal: What does a cameraman filming his own settlement see differently?
ref: Rohingya
A Muslim community of Myanmar's Rakhine state whom Myanmar does not recognise as citizens. Since the 2017 military crackdown most are refugees in Bangladesh.
Al Jazeera World
Al Jazeera's long-form documentary series, which tells stories from the Arab world and the Global South.

h: Meeting Muktibodh on the street, and the question of the literature fest
dek: In Ashutosh Chandan's satirical tale, Muktibodh meets the narrator on a Delhi street and asks why writers are going to the festival of a channel that spreads hatred.
body: This piece by theatre artist and poet Ashutosh Chandan is something between an essay and a story. On a Delhi street, the narrator suddenly runs into Gajanan Madhav Muktibodh. He thinks that a silent poet is more unsettling than a shouting revolutionary, because his silence may hold a wound or it may hold cunning. He decides Muktibodh is the first kind and, nervously, speaks to him.

Muktibodh looks into his eyes for a long time and then points to a procession. Ahead, writers, novelists, critics, actors, singers and journalists are heading in cars towards Dhyan Chand Stadium, where a channel's literature festival is on. Muktibodh asks how writers can celebrate at the gala of a channel that spreads hatred and lies during the student movement, the farmers' movement and all year round.

The narrator's answer is cool and clever. In his view, knowledge, feeling and art are now tools of business, a person's work and his image are polished separately, and Muktibodh's time is over. Muktibodh says ideas do not die. To dodge the point, the narrator starts reciting something like an advertisement for mint cigarettes.

Then Muktibodh bends towards his left slipper. The narrator fears he is about to be hit, but it turns out Muktibodh was looking at its coming-apart stitching. From here the narrator starts putting a price on his own conscience and decides he will sell it only after he becomes famous, because an ordinary man's conscience fetches little.

In the end that same slipper flies up and beats him, and he wakes up dozing in a library. Beside him a student is cramming objective-type Hindi questions for a permanent job, and on a pile of books lies a copy of Andhere Mein (In the Dark).
nazar: The target of the satire is clear: the Hindi literary world that climbs onto the stage of media houses busy with the ruling power's propaganda without asking questions. The sharpest part of the story is the narrator's confession, which puts the reader in the dock too. The ending, with the jobless student and the copy of Andhere Mein, says the question of commitment still lies buried in a pile of books.
sawal: On whose head should Muktibodh's torn slipper land today?
ref: Gajanan Madhav Muktibodh
A major Hindi poet and critic (1917-1964) who, living in want, raised the question of the intellectual's commitment.
Andhere Mein
Muktibodh's long poem (In the Dark), counted among the most discussed works in Hindi on power, fear and the silence of intellectuals.
photo_note: English babu holding a hookah, Kalighat painting

h: From children broken by paper leaks to old friends: poems by Sanjay Rai
dek: Sammukh has published six poems by Kolkata poet Sanjay Rai, carrying both the grief of the NEET paper leak and the fading conversation in relationships.
body: Sammukh has published six poems by Sanjay Rai on the occasion of his wedding, with a short editorial note. Sanjay Rai is an assistant professor at Seth Anandram Jaipuria College in Kolkata, and the magazine describes his poetry as one of tender personal feeling. The poems are not reproduced here; this is only an introduction.

The first poem, Ubalti Hui Chuppi (Boiling Silence), connects most directly with public grief. It is an elegy for the children who took their lives during the NEET paper leak. The poem sets the movement, as a silence made of everyone's voices together, against suicide, as the silence of one person alone.

Purane Dost (Old Friends) is a long poem that builds its images from everyday modern things: nicotine in the city's blood, a dry kulhad (clay cup), a mobile data pack, fountain pen ink and a dying battery. In it, old friends do not change life; they repair it.

In Ek Sadharan Katha (An Ordinary Tale), the speaker refuses a showy, extraordinary identity and wants to become an ordinary story that power cannot use. The poem asks how religion and history become tools of politics. Baat Ab Nahin Hoti (We Don't Talk Anymore) shows the difference between the deep, few-worded conversations of old days and today's silence full of many words.

Spam and Apurn Vakya (Incomplete Sentence) are short poems. In one, a relationship is like an email lying in spam that the receiver never learns about; in the other, between the sky and the mud there is only a missing case marker.
nazar: The strength of these poems is that private tenderness and public grief walk together in one set. Scams like paper leaks end up as figures in the newspaper; poetry turns them back into the silence of children. The insistence on being ordinary is also a small but clear statement against today's identity politics.
sawal: Who will hear the silence of children broken by paper leaks?
ref: NEET
The national entrance exam for medical colleges, whose paper leak allegations troubled lakhs of students and families.
Case marker
In Hindi grammar, markers such as ka, ko, se and mein that show the relationship between words.
photo_note: Lady in the Moonlight, Raja Ravi Varma

h: Six centuries of Ahom rule that school history forgot
dek: Manisha Kulshreshtha calls Jyotsna Mishra's book Swarn, Rakt aur Brahma-putra a book that fills a real gap in Hindi on the history of Assam.
body: Fiction writer Manisha Kulshreshtha has reviewed Dr Jyotsna Mishra's book Swarn, Rakt aur Brahma-putra (Gold, Blood and the Brahmaputra) on Jankipul. It is published by Penguin Swadesh and runs to 226 pages. The reviewer's first question is why the Ahom kingdom, which ruled a large part of Assam for so long, found no place in the history taught in schools.

According to the review, the book covers nearly six centuries, from the journey of Sukapha to the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826, and also goes back to seventh-century Kamarupa and Bhaskarvarman. Sukapha set out from Yunnan in search of a land of golden gardens and, after wandering for about thirteen years, settled in the Brahmaputra valley. According to the author, his lasting rule was built not on conquest but on a policy of dialogue and harmony with local tribes.

The book does not tell events in straight date order. The story begins in 1817 at Sirimari, where the exiled Purandar Singh is told the whole history by his grandfather. Through this conversation come the paik system, Shankardev's Neo-Vaishnava movement, Lachit Barphukan's victory over the Mughals at Saraighat in 1671, the Moamoria rebellion and the Burmese invasions. According to the reviewer, the British won Assam not through war but through diplomacy.

The gold and blood of the title are not decoration: on one side are state-building, prosperity and culture, on the other conspiracy, wars of succession and violence. The river, the rain and the land also appear as characters that shape politics. The author has drawn on the Ahom chronicles called buranjis, travel accounts, archaeology and Assamese and English sources.
Manisha admits that despite living in the Northeast for seven years she knew very little about the Ahom kingdom, and the book enriched her.
nazar: The sense of history in the Hindi belt often stays stuck on the throne of Delhi, and the Northeast becomes a footnote in the margin. Books like this remind us that this country's political story was made from many centres. The Ahom kingdom, which lasted through harmony, is also a lesson for today's majoritarian history writing.
sawal: Why has Lachit of Saraighat stayed out of Hindi textbooks until now?
ref: Ahom dynasty
A kingdom founded by Sukapha in the thirteenth century, which ruled the Brahmaputra valley of Assam until 1826.
Buranji
History chronicles written at the Ahom court, a major source for the medieval history of Assam.

h: The trap of motivational reels, and gratitude, the hardest motivation
dek: In his column Reel Rasacharya, Rachit asks when people who watch one motivational reel and book after another will actually get to work.
body: This time, Rachit's column Reel Rasacharya (Master of Reel Flavours) on Hindwi's Bela is about motivational reels. The writer says he watches heaps of motivational clips with poetry and music, but none of them makes him stop scrolling and go to work. His question is simple: if people keep watching one motivational video after another, when will the work get done?

The same goes for readers of self-help books. A friend of the writer is a fan of Robin Sharma; while reading The 5 AM Club he began to think himself fit to be President, and lately he was being drawn towards an MLM company's seminar. According to the writer, reading book after book is the same loop as watching reel after reel, where you feel victorious through someone else's imagined success and the real effort keeps getting put off.

His argument is that motivation comes from within. Books can teach skills and time management, just as the craft of poetry can be taught but not the feeling of poetry. The cheapest motivation is the sense of being a victim, where some villain provides the fuel, and once the villain is gone the zeal goes too.

The hardest motivation, according to the writer, is gratitude, which lies at the root of almost all great art. For this he cites the poetry of Naveen Sagar and Neeraj, where instead of revenge there is a wish to turn sorrow into song.
Finally, with a line from George Carlin and the example of Macbeth, he reminds us that highly motivated people have also waged wars and committed murders, so purpose matters more than motivation.
nazar: This piece says a serious thing in a light way: the motivation market is now an industry stretching from MLM to algorithms, profiting by selling restlessness. The Macbeth example is the most useful, because the question is always what the zeal is for.
sawal: How did the friend reading The 5 AM Club end up at an MLM seminar?
ref: MLM
Multi-level marketing, where earnings depend more on recruiting new members than on selling goods.
George Carlin
American stand-up comedian (1937-2008), known for sharp satire on power, religion and consumerism.

h: In the flesh trade, why is the woman shamed and the male buyer free?
dek: Shivani's essay asks why, in the debate on prostitution, only the woman stands in the dock, when the market runs on men's demand.
body: Shivani's essay begins with a childhood memory. Seeing women standing by the roadside in big cities at dusk for the first time, she was frightened. Later her understanding grew through films, news and the streets of Delhi, and the writer says that at first she too had assumed the girls were to blame.

Then she questions her own judgement. There are two people in this transaction, so why is only one blamed? The men who run the market and go there live in society as respectable people, and among boys they are praised as real men or players. The writer asks why men who run this market, or who form relationships through emotional deceit, are not counted within the bounds of male prostitution.

She sees the same double standard in history and literature. The nagarvadhu and the ganika appear in old texts, but their wealthy patrons were called connoisseurs, not shamed. Films like Gangubai, Devdas and Kalank show women's suffering, but according to the writer they leave out the whole truth: that women are pushed into this trade by helplessness and social traps, and that the real issue is men's demand.

She sees the root in upbringing. Girls are taught fear in the name of honour and propriety; boys are not taught to respect other people's bodies and feelings. The writer also tells of a motherless girl who was abused by her own father, and says that this violence of the market and of the home comes from the same gaze.
The essay concludes that before blaming any woman, an account should be demanded of men's character.
nazar: This essay turns the debate around, which is needed: both law and society have so far treated the woman trapped in the trade as the criminal and the buyer as invisible. Without talking about demand, no serious policy on human trafficking and sexual exploitation can be made. The part on upbringing is the most solid, because change will begin there.
sawal: If the nagarvadhu was shamed, why did her connoisseur patron stay safe?
ref: Nagarvadhu
In ancient India, a celebrated dancer or courtesan of the city, such as Amrapali of Vaishali.
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act
A 1956 law that makes running brothels and trafficking a crime, though there has been debate that its blows fall mostly on women.
photo_note: Group of Three Girls, Amrita Sher-Gil

h: Poems by Turkish poet Nisa Leyla, from Ariadne's thread to war
dek: Samalochan presents seven poems by contemporary Turkish poet Nisa Leyla, translated into Hindi from the original Turkish by Nishant Kaushik.
body: Samalochan has published seven poems by Turkish poet, writer and editor Nisa Leyla, translated into Hindi from the original Turkish. The translation is by Nishant Kaushik, who was born in Jabalpur, studied at Jamia Millia Islamia and translates into Hindi from Persian, Turkish, Urdu, Azerbaijani and English. According to the magazine, the poems were chosen with the poet's consent. The poems are not reproduced here; this is only an introduction.

Nisa Leyla was born in Iskenderun in 1972, studied English and economics at Cukurova University, taught English for three years and worked in government administration for five years. She has five poetry collections, including a book for children, and a memoir called Adana's Dreams. She has received the Mevlut Kaplan Literature Award and an honour at an art festival in Italy for her poem Peace (Rain).

According to the introduction, her poetry grapples with love, separation, memory, sadness, irony and questions of existence, and is experimental, image-rich poetry full of Greek myths and philosophical references.

The first poem in the selection makes Ariadne's mythical thread a symbol of escaping the dark and of the road to freedom. Gunshots Louder Than the Chirping holds up the hope of love, democracy and peace against war and violence, and strikes at the hypocrisy of power. Salt is a poem of companionship and trust, Mermaid one of a lost self and the freedom of the sea.

I Miss You So Much begins with personal longing and spreads to war and the solidarity of women with one another, and in Pour Out a Mayakovsky the revolutionary legacy of poetry is recalled through Mayakovsky and Adnan Yucel.
nazar: Contemporary Turkish poetry reaches Hindi almost entirely through the personal devotion of translators, so this offering is precious. At a time when news of war arrives every day, a Turkish poet's image of gunshots and chirping will feel to the Hindi reader like their own unease.
sawal: In the noise of gunfire, by what thread does the Turkish poet search for democracy?
ref: Ariadne
A princess of Greek myth, with the help of whose thread Theseus found his way out of the labyrinth.
Mayakovsky
Vladimir Mayakovsky (1893-1930), poet of the Russian Revolution era, whose poetry became an example for progressive poets around the world.
